To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

monoclonal antibodies specific to the five major glycopeptides of herpes simplex type 1 (HSV-1) are effective in promoting recovery of mice from HVS-1 infection when given intravenously 4 to 48 hours after corneal infection.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a vaccine for the treatment of herpes simplex virus (HSV) ocular infection.
the development of a new therapeutic approach to ocular herpes.
the development of monoclonal antibody therapy for HSV-1-induced keratoconjunctivitis in humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

antibodies to the HSV-1 glycoproteins can mediate immunity to HSV-1 infection, and that the protective activity of a specific monoclone does not correlate with the in vitro immunological reactivity of the monoclone.
antibodies to the glycoproteins are effective in promoting recovery, but the mechanism of this protection is not understood.
the monoclonal antibody to glycoprotein gB was the only one that was effective in all three immunologic assays, while the other antibodies were effective only in one or two of the immunologic assays.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
monoclonal antibodies specific to the HSV-1 glycoproteins, gC, A/B, D, and E, can be used to protect against ocular HSV- 1 disease.
the monoclonal antibody specific for glycoprotein gA/B was the most effective in mediating protection from corneal disease.

antibodies can interact with glycoproteins to promote recovery from HSV- 1 infection in vivo, and the immunologic reactivity of the antibodies in vitro is not predictive of the protective activity of these antibodies in vivo.
The main takeaway from our work is that

monoclonal antibodies are useful tools for the analysis of antibody-mediated immunity to HSV-1 ocular infection, and that in vitro immunological reactivity does not necessarily predict the in vivo effectiveness of a given antibody.
the protective effect of a monoclonal antibody in vivo does not correlate with any of the in vitro assays of immunological reactivity.
the use of monoclonal antibody in the treatment of ocular HSV- 1 infection should be evaluated in the context of in vivo protection from disease.
